```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

CrateDB is a distributed SQL database for analytics and operational data.
Use `oauth_db_cratedb_api()` to run SQL through CrateDB's HTTPS interface
with each visitor's JWT access token. CrateDB maps the token to a database
user and enforces that user's privileges. This is an HTTP query client;
CrateDB's JWT authentication does not work through its PostgreSQL interface.

## Try CrateDB locally

With Docker running:

```{r demo}
shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_demo("cratedb")
```

The demo includes CrateDB 6.4.3, Keycloak, a Shiny app and read-only database
users. Alice and Bob can read a shared table; **Try a write** checks that
CrateDB rejects their writes. See [Local Docker demos](local-demos.html)
for accounts and cleanup.

CrateDB expects the token's issuer URL to serve its public signing keys.
The demo's HTTPS gateway supplies those keys at Keycloak's issuer URL while
forwarding normal browser sign-in to Keycloak. It passes the original
access token to CrateDB. Inspect `cratedb/server.py` and
`realm-extended.json` with `oauth_db_demo("cratedb", action = "files")`
for the complete setup.

## Collect the connection settings

Your server must enable JWT authentication for its HTTP SQL interface.
The required user claims and configuration follow the app example.

| Setting | Where to get it |
| --- | --- |
| `url` | CrateDB's HTTP endpoint with `/_sql`, exposed through HTTPS |
| `schema` and table | Your database's schema and table names, often `doc` |
| `OAUTHDB_CRATEDB_ISSUER` | Your compatible OAuth provider's issuer URL |
| Client ID and secret | The [Shiny app registration](oauth-setup.html) in that provider |

Put the `OAUTHDB_*` values in `.Renviron` and restart R. CrateDB needs a
`username` claim and specific signing-key discovery; check the setup section
before reusing tokens from an existing provider.

## A complete app

This example assumes an OIDC provider configured to issue compatible JWT
access tokens. Replace the SQL endpoint and table for your deployment.
Add the provider's API scopes, resource or named token target to the client
as needed. Pass `target` and `required_scopes` to the helper when using them.
CrateDB's user grants remain the authority for data access.

```{r app}
library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(
  issuer = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CRATEDB_ISSUER")
)
client <- oauth_client(
  provider,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile")
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server("auth", client, auto_redirect = FALSE)
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  crate <- oauth_db_cratedb_api(
    auth$connection,
    url = "https://crate.example.org:4200/_sql",
    schema = "doc"
  )
  output$rows <- renderTable({
    crate$query(
      "SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE country = $1 LIMIT 20",
      parameters = list("NL")
    )
  })
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*"),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

# Open the app in your regular browser at http://localhost:8100
# (viewers in RStudio/Positron/etc. cannot perform necessary redirects)
```

Run `source("example.R")`. The app waits for sign-in before querying
and clears the output on sign-out. Use `ca_bundle` for a private CA.


## Configure CrateDB and compatible token claims

Enable host-based authentication and configure `method: jwt` rules with
`protocol: http` for the intended users. Expose `/_sql` through verified
TLS, either directly on CrateDB or through a reverse proxy. For example,
an HTTP rule for Alice in `crate.yml` looks like this:

```yaml
auth.host_based.enabled: true
auth.host_based.config:
  alice:
    user: alice
    method: jwt
    protocol: http
```

Keep separate administrative authentication rules appropriate to your
deployment. Create the database user and grant only the privileges needed:

```sql
CREATE USER alice WITH (jwt = {
  "iss" = 'https://identity.example.org/',
  "username" = 'alice',
  "aud" = 'reporting-api'
});
GRANT DQL ON TABLE doc.orders TO alice;
```

The access token must have matching `iss`, `username` and `aud` claims,
a `kid` header and a signing key CrateDB can obtain from the provider's
JWK endpoint. Configure token expiry with `exp`. In particular, CrateDB
expects `username`; a provider returning only `sub` or `preferred_username`
needs a suitable claim mapping. Its JWT documentation describes `iss` as
the JWK endpoint. Verify key discovery with your provider and CrateDB
version before using the app; the helper does not rewrite token claims
or exchange an incompatible token.

Global `auth.host_based.jwt.iss` settings override per-user JWT properties.
See the server's [JWT authentication documentation](https://cratedb.com/docs/crate/reference/en/latest/admin/auth/methods.html#jwt-authentication-method)
and [user settings](https://cratedb.com/docs/crate/reference/en/latest/sql/statements/create-user.html).

Register an OAuth client with the identity provider. Allow
`http://localhost:8100` as its development redirect URI, and configure the
access-token audience and claims required above. Save your registration
in `.Renviron` and restart R:

```text
OAUTHDB_CRATEDB_ISSUER=https://identity.example.org/
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret
```


## Parameters, results and lifetime

Use `$1`, `$2`, ... or `?` placeholders with an unnamed list of parameters.
Values are sent as JSON separately from SQL; named lists inside a parameter
represent objects, and unnamed lists or atomic vectors represent arrays.
Missing values become JSON null. Dates and POSIXct timestamps become ISO
strings, with timestamps expressed in UTC. Cast the placeholders to the
desired SQL types. For exact numbers, pass strings and cast them explicitly:

```{r exact-query}
crate$query(
  "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1::bigint",
  parameters = list("9007199254740993")
)
```

BIGINT and NUMERIC results remain strings, preserving their exact digits.
Smaller numeric columns become R numbers and booleans become logical.
Timestamps and dates retain epoch-millisecond strings. Arrays, objects and
other complex types remain list columns with numbers represented as strings.
Empty results keep their types; duplicate column names stay unchanged.
Use `$query(..., raw = TRUE)` for column metadata and the original row layout.
`$execute()` invisibly returns the affected row count, or `-1` when unknown.

shinyOAuth obtains or renews a token before each request. Account changes,
lost required scopes, sign-out and session end stop local access. A response
arriving after its authorization changes is discarded. The helper never
replays SQL after a 401, redirect, timeout or other failure. A statement
may already have changed data even if its response was lost, so check the
server outcome before manually resubmitting a write.

## Run the real-server checks

The source repository includes a
[CrateDB Docker fixture](https://github.com/lukakoning/shinyOAuthDB/tree/main/integration/cratedb-oauth)
with signed visitor tokens, native CrateDB JWT validation and a TLS proxy.
From the checkout root, run `Rscript tools/check-cratedb-oauth.R` with Docker
running and the test dependencies installed. No production credentials are
needed. The checks cover user privileges, exact types, token changes,
rejected credentials, TLS verification and lost write responses.
